summary: Gives a new, accurate definition of DNS zone transfer (AXFR), one of the ways authoritative name servers keep their zone data in sync. The older definition in RFC 1034 and RFC 1035 lacked detail, so this records how interoperable implementations actually behave. It is a Proposed Standard.

eli5.summary: When a helper copy of a phone book needs the whole book, AXFR hands over every page. This writes down exactly how that copy works.

questions: how does dns zone transfer work
what is the difference between axfr and ixfr
subtitle: How a DNS server hands a complete copy of a zone to another server over TCP, written down the way it really works.

tldr.problem: The original description of AXFR was scattered across RFC 1034 and RFC 1035 and lacked detail, so implementers had to guess, which hurt interoperability.
tldr.mechanism: A client sends one AXFR query over TCP for a zone. The server replies with a series of DNS messages that begins and ends with the zone's SOA record and carries every record of the zone in between.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5936 is a Proposed Standard that records the interoperable behavior and updates RFC 1034 and RFC 1035. It has itself been updated by RFC 9103.

today: RFC 5936 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 1034 and RFC 1035, and it has been updated by RFC 9103. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why AXFR Needed a Rewrite
sections.content:
The DNS has three standard ways to keep the authoritative name servers of a zone in step: AXFR (a full zone transfer, defined in RFC 1034 and RFC 1035), IXFR (incremental transfer, RFC 1995) and NOTIFY (prompt notice of zone changes, RFC 1996). Their shared goal is to let a set of name servers remain coherently authoritative for a zone.

The original AXFR definition is scattered through RFC 1034 and RFC 1035 and proved insufficient in detail, so implementations had to make assumptions. The abstract notes that, even so, a satisfactory set of implementations interoperate today. This document is a new definition only in the sense that it records an accurate description of that interoperable behavior.

The scope is deliberately narrow. It covers AXFR only, leaving IXFR and NOTIFY to other documents. It does not cover deliberately incoherent DNS setups, and it says a DNS implementation is not required to support AXFR at all, although it should have some means of keeping its servers coherent.
sections.eli5: Two helpers both keep a copy of the same phone book. The old rules for swapping a whole copy were vague, so this paper writes down how it really works.

sections.title: The AXFR Query
sections.content:
An AXFR session is one query plus the series of response messages it triggers. The sender of the query is the AXFR client and the responder is the AXFR server. Terms such as master or slave do not matter for defining AXFR.

The query is an ordinary DNS message with tightly fixed header values: QR must be 0, OPCODE must be 0 (standard query), RCODE must be 0, QDCOUNT must be 1, and ANCOUNT and NSCOUNT must be 0. The client picks an ID that it is not already using with that server.

The single Question names the zone in QNAME, uses QTYPE AXFR (252), and gives the zone's class in QCLASS. The Additional section may carry one EDNS OPT record and one transaction security record, currently TSIG or SIG(0). If a server does not understand the OPT record, the client must retry without it. A FormErr(1) reply is the usual hint.
sections.eli5: The question is a short, strictly formatted note: 'Please send me the whole zone called this.' The note has no room for extras, apart from an optional ID card to prove who is asking.

sections.title: The AXFR Response
sections.content:
The response is a series of DNS messages, which may be a series of length one. The first message must begin with the zone's SOA record and the last message must conclude with the same SOA record. Intermediate messages must not contain the SOA. The server copies the Question into the first response message; later messages may copy it or leave it empty.

Apart from the SOA at the start and end, the zone is treated as an unordered set of records. Servers usually keep related records together, but clients must accept any ordering and grouping of the non-SOA records. Each record should be sent once, and clients must ignore duplicates. Responses should pack in as many records as fit, but because some old clients expect one record per message, a server may be configured to send a single record each time.

Header rules for responses: the ID is copied from the query, QR is 1, OPCODE is 0, TC must be 0, and AA must be 1 when RCODE is 0. A server that is not authoritative for the zone should answer NotAuth(9). An error ends the session with a single message that carries the Question and the error code; it does not need the closing SOA. The 65535-octet limit from the two-byte TCP length prefix is the only size limit on a message.
sections.eli5: The server sends the phone book in batches. The first batch starts with the cover page, the last batch ends with the same cover page, and the pages in between can come in any order.

sections.title: What the Zone Transfer Contains
sections.content:
The goal of a transfer is to let the client faithfully reconstruct the zone as it exists at the primary server for a given serial number, meaning the content that is actually served, not how the server stores it. Zones that are impractical to list in full for one serial number, such as ones generated from ever-changing data, are not suitable for AXFR.

Delegation records. The response must contain the NS record set at a zone cut exactly as registered with the zone being transferred, whether or not it matches the authoritative set in the child zone. This exposes inconsistencies to an administrator, avoids forcing the server to run extra queries, and ensures that a given zone and serial number always yields the same records from any server. That property matters for incremental transfers such as IXFR. Glue records registered with the zone must be included in the same way, for any address family.

Names and compression. Name compression in an AXFR message should be case-preserving, so that a and A are not treated as equal for compression purposes. This is a deliberate departure from normal DNS name comparison.

Occluded names. Names hidden below a delegation or a DNAME added by dynamic update must still be included, and clients must be able to handle them. The stated reason is quick recovery if the update was a mistake.
sections.eli5: The copy has to match the original exactly, even the odd bits, and even the pages that are currently hidden, so that nothing is lost if someone wants to undo a change.

sections.title: Transport: TCP Only
sections.content:
AXFR is restricted to TCP. RFC 1034 says that because accuracy is essential, TCP or some other reliable protocol must be used. This document does not define AXFR over UDP, because some aspects of a session do not translate easily to it.

The old assumption that a TCP connection carries exactly one AXFR session is described as incorrect. A client may send an SOA query first on the same connection, reuse an open connection for other queries, and run several transfers at once, which is why servers must copy the query ID into every response. Reusing an open connection is recommended over opening a new one.

Closing the connection is the only way to cancel a transfer, and it cancels everything else on that connection too. If the connection is closed remotely, the client must cancel all outstanding sessions and should avoid endless or ever faster retries. A server must handle several AXFR sessions on one connection, and should close a connection only in reaction to limits or in extreme security cases.
sections.eli5: AXFR uses a phone line that stays connected until the whole book is read out, not postcards that might get lost. You can ask for several books on one call.

sections.title: Authorization and Zone Integrity
sections.content:
Zone administrators may restrict who can use AXFR. The RFC acknowledges that this was not part of the original design but has become a practical need. A DNS implementation should provide a way to limit AXFR to specific clients, such as by IP address ranges, and a general-purpose implementation is recommended to support access control based on TSIG or SIG(0). It should be possible to open access to all requests, but a general-purpose implementation should not make that the default.

On the receiving side, the client must make sure that only a fully and successfully transferred copy is ever used to serve the zone. The model is two-stage: save the data as it arrives, then, after the transfer completes and sanity checks pass, load it atomically. If anything goes wrong, the partial data must be deleted and the client keeps serving the previous version. A rejected zone version may be fetched again, possibly from another server.

The document says it adds no new security considerations beyond those of RFC 1034 and RFC 1035, and points to RFC 3833 for DNS threats in general. Where transfers cross the public Internet, TSIG or SIG(0) lets clients verify the contents.
sections.eli5: Not everybody should get a full copy of the phone book, so the owner can choose who may ask. And the helper only swaps in the new copy once every page has arrived intact.

sections.title: Dealing with Older Software
sections.content:
Because the original definition was vague, older clients and servers behave in varied ways. Backwards compatibility is not required, but the more an implementation supports, the better it interoperates. Turnkey implementations usually do not need to care.

The one thing a server cannot discover about a client is whether the client can only accept a single record per message, so it has to be set by configuration. If an implementation allows that setting per client, the default should be multiple records per message. Clients should be careful not to let extra queries on a TCP connection interrupt the original request.

Because the need to fall back cannot be detected, implementations are told to encourage operators to review the clients and servers they have made notes about, since old software gets updated over time. The only IANA action was to add a reference to this RFC at the AXFR (252) entry of the DNS Resource Record TYPEs registry.
sections.eli5: Some old helpers can only handle one page at a time, and there is no way to tell, so someone has to write it on a note. The note should be checked now and then.
